1:
Gill places the word seven days before the flood, the ark built and everything ready. Ellicott fills in what the week was for — the building over, the remaining days spent collecting the animals before Noah takes up his abode. He corrects a common misreading too: many suppose a hundred and twenty years were spent on the work, but that rests on an untenable reading of an earlier verse which really fixes the duration of human life. Henry fastens on the wording of the summons and gets the best of the chapter from it. God does not bid Noah go into the ark but come into it, implying that God would go with him, lead him in, keep him company, and in due time bring him out; and that presence made the ark — a prison in itself — not merely a refuge but a palace. He notes too that Noah did not enter until bidden: knowing what the vessel was for, he still waited for a renewed command, and had it. The invitation extends to the household, and Henry will not tidy away what that involved. One son was Ham, who proved a bad man and was yet saved in the ark — whence he draws that wicked children often fare better for godly parents' sake, and that there is a mixture of bad with good in the best societies: in Noah's family a Ham, in Christ's a Judas, no perfect purity this side of heaven.

Calvin measures what the command cost. Noah had sustained a hundred years of the fiercest assaults, but the severest contest was this — to bid farewell to the world, renounce society, and bury himself in the ark. The timing made it harder. The face of the earth was lovely just then, the season when herbs shoot and trees flourish, winter and its frost gone; God chose the very spring to destroy the world. It was no light trial to leave the only life he had known for six hundred years and seek a new one in the abyss of death — commanded to forsake the world and live in a sepulchre he had spent a century laboriously digging for himself. Nothing confirmed the warning. All around him men feasted, celebrated marriages, built sumptuous houses, as Christ himself testifies that the age was intoxicated with its pleasures. So the Lord fortified his servant by renewing the promise, telling him not to wait till the veins of the earth burst and the cataracts of heaven rushed down, but to enter while all was tranquil and remain seven days.

The commendation given as the reason for the rescue Henry and Wesley handle in nearly identical words. Those are righteous indeed who are righteous before God — having not only the form of godliness, by which they appear righteous to men easily imposed upon, but the power of it, by which they approve themselves to God who searches the heart. Henry adds that in a world of wicked people God could see one righteous Noah: that grain of wheat could not be lost, not in so great a heap of chaff. God is especially pleased with those good in bad times, which made Noah illustriously righteous. Calvin sees a difficulty in the same sentence. If Noah was saved because he was righteous, it seems to follow that we may deserve life by works. His first answer is that the design was to set one man against the whole world, so that in his person the unrighteousness of all might be condemned. His second is that accepting a man's righteousness is not repugnant to free acceptance, since God accepts gifts he himself conferred: he loves men freely, finding nothing in them but what deserves hatred, adopts them in Christ, justifies them by mercy, and only then regenerates them — from which good works flow afterwards, not before.
2:
That the distinction of clean and unclean is made here at all strikes every commentator, since it long precedes the law of Moses. Gill infers it was known before the flood, grounding it in the practice of sacrificing ever since the fall — men having been taught by revelation both to sacrifice and what to offer. Clarke says the same, that the distinction marked which animals were proper for sacrifice and food. Ellicott is more careful about what it cannot mean: there can be no reference to the Levitical law, which had respect to human food, nor to a division between tame and wild, since all alike are called cattle; the clean were probably those which from Adam and Abel had been offered in sacrifice — oxen, sheep and goats — the unclean such beasts as camels, horses and asses. How many were taken is disputed. Ellicott thinks seven of each kind rather than seven pairs, arguing that otherwise few species could have been included, since attending to so large a number would have been beyond Noah and his sons. Calvin and Keil agree on the number but divide it differently, making three pairs with a single animal added for sacrifice; Calvin notes Le Clerc objected and supposed seven of each sex, suspecting a scepticism about the seventh animal's use lay behind it.

Ellicott alone raises the documentary question, and handles it evenly. These fuller orders are given in the name of Jehovah, whereas most of the flood narrative is Elohistic, from which some assume a Jehovist completed an earlier account — the additions being this chapter's opening verses, the shutting of the door, Noah's sacrifice, and the cursing of Canaan. Ellicott's counter comes from outside the text: the sacrifice is as integral to the Chaldean Genesis as the sending forth of the birds, and so indubitably older than Moses. Yet he does not dismiss the case. There is nothing improbable in Moses having had two records of the flood before him; and though the Elohistic and Jehovistic division of Genesis usually breaks down, there is at least a prima facie appearance of two narratives combined here.

On the seven days' delay Gill reports three explanations — mourning for Methuselah, an addition to the years granted for repentance, or simply time for Noah to settle his family and the creatures — and prefers the last. Clarke suggests the word was spoken on a sabbath, and follows the forty days forward: the period became sacred and proper for humiliation, in the fasts of Moses and Elijah and our Lord, in the respite given to Nineveh, and at length in Lent. Ellicott makes the point more compactly: forty became the sacred number of trial and patience, the length of the fast in the wilderness and of the sojourn after the Resurrection. Wesley turns the delay into a warning. God granted a reprieve of seven days more, to show how slow he is to anger and give further space for repentance; but it was all in vain, and those days were trifled away like the rest. Noah had told them of judgment at a distance and they put off repenting; now he must tell them it is at the door — and it is common, Wesley adds, for men careless of their souls through years of health, when death looked far off, to be as careless through the seven days of their sickness, when they see it approaching. Henry marks the obedience that answers it: Noah went in on notice, though no cloud threatened and all was serene, walking at every step by faith and not by sense. Calvin adds that this is no bare repetition but a commendation of Noah's uniform obedience — in whatever particular it pleased God to try him he remained constant, since it is not becoming to obey one commandment only and then feel free to withdraw.
6:
The age is repeated, and Calvin thinks not without reason. Old age has this among its other evils, that it makes men more indolent and morose; so Noah's faith is the more conspicuous for not failing him at that advanced period, and if it was a great excellence not to languish through successive centuries, his promptitude deserves its own commendation, since being commanded to enter he obeyed at once. Calvin also guards the phrase that he went in because of the waters of the flood. It does not mean he was driven in by the rush of the water, but that being moved by the word he perceived through faith the approach of a deluge which everyone else was ridiculing — his faith is commended here precisely because he raised his eyes above heaven and earth. Gill works out the arithmetic, that Noah was six hundred when it began and in his six hundred and first year when it ended, his eldest son by then a hundred years old. Ellicott follows the same reckoning and adds a detail easily missed: Shem was about a hundred and his brothers younger, and all three were married, though apparently as yet without children.

How the animals were gathered Moses now explains, and the answer is that they came of their own accord. Calvin knows this sounds absurd and meets it by looking back: in the beginning every kind presented itself to Adam that he might name them, and we dread the sight of wild beasts for no other reason than that, having shaken off the yoke of God, we have lost the authority with which Adam was endued. What happened here was a kind of restoration of that former state, God bringing to Noah the animals he intended to preserve by Noah's labour — so that untamed creatures were kept in the ark much as hens and geese are kept in a coop. Calvin will not let the point rest on the animals either. It was humanly impossible that such an assemblage should be made in a moment; but because Noah simply trusted the outcome to God and did what was enjoined, God gave power to his own precept, which was in effect a promise annexed to the command. Noah's faith, Calvin concludes, availed more than all snares and nets for the capture of animals, and by that very same gate lions and wolves and tigers entered meekly along with oxen and lambs. Wesley says it in one line: the same hand that at first brought them to Adam to be named now brought them to Noah to be preserved. Gill allows two explanations, that they came impressed with an instinct from God, or by the ministry of angels.

Ellicott closes the section by setting the story beside its Babylonian counterpart, where Xisuthrus takes aboard not only wild animals but seeds of every kind of plant, gold and silver, and slaves both male and female — the sons of the best and the sons of the people. There a whole tribe is saved with their chief; here one family only. On the seven days he passes on the Jewish tradition that they were the days of mourning for Methuselah, who died in the year of the flood. Calvin returns at the same point to the question of the month, since the Hebrews begin their year in March for sacred things and in September for common affairs, the two equinoxes giving them a double commencement; but because the sacred reckoning was divinely appointed and is besides more agreeable to nature, he judges it probable that the deluge began about the time of spring.
11:
The date is given with a precision the commentators think deliberate, and they check it against the other numbers. Gill reads the six hundredth year as current, not complete, Noah having lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood and not fifty-one; Clarke reaches the same from the other end, counting the year in the ark and the death at nine hundred and fifty. Henry sets it at 1656 years from the creation and draws a note from the reckoning: the years of the old world are numbered not by the reigns of giants but by the lives of patriarchs, saints being of more account with God than princes. On the month all agree against Calvin. Clarke identifies the first month as Tisri and the second as Marcheshvan, the change of the year's beginning to Nisan having come only after the deliverance from Egypt. Ellicott adds the reason — the ecclesiastical year beginning in Abib commemorates that deliverance and can have no place here — so the flood began toward the end of October and lasted till spring. Henry and Wesley, reckoning it about the beginning of November, notice a homely consequence: Noah had a harvest just before, to victual the ark. Ellicott proves the year lunar besides, the hundred and fifty days of prevailing running from the seventeenth of the second month to the seventeenth of the seventh — five months of thirty each.

Calvin frames the two causes by going back to the creation. The earth was originally covered with water, and by God's singular kindness the waters receded so that space might be left for living creatures — a thing philosophers must admit is contrary to nature, and which Scripture reckons among God's miracles. God raised for men a theatre in the habitable region of the earth, causing that the subterranean waters should not break out nor the celestial conspire with them. Now those barriers were torn up. And here Calvin sets down the sentence that governs the passage: God might have deposited in veins of the earth as much water as human life required, but has designedly placed us between two graves, lest in fancied security we despise the kindness our life depends on — for the element philosophers count a principle of life threatens us with death from above and beneath, except so far as God's hand restrains it. Henry and Wesley put the thought in the language of storehouses. There needed no new creation of waters: God had laid up the deep in store and now broke it up, removing the mounds and fences set at the creation, so the sea returned to cover the earth as at first. The rain that ordinarily descends in drops came down in streams; God binds the waters in his thick clouds and the cloud is not rent, but now the bond was loosed.

Clarke ventures a physical account: an immense quantity of water occupied the centre of the antediluvian earth, and as it burst forth the surrounding strata must have sunk to fill the vacuum; he derives the word rendered flood from a root meaning to confound. Ellicott is more cautious about the language and bolder about the event. The description is usually taken for extraordinary rain in the narrator's popular idiom; but the words suggest a great cosmic catastrophe by which some vast body of water was set loose, and without such a convulsion it is hard to see how the ark, a vessel incapable of sailing, could have gone against the current up to the watershed of Ararat. He adds a quantitative objection: the earth's annual evaporation being fixed, its downpour concentrated into forty days would scarcely produce so vast a deluge. Henry ends where the arithmetic began — God made the world in six days but was forty destroying it, for he is slow to anger; yet it came effectually.
12:
Calvin asks why the waters were not loosed at once, and gives two reasons. Partly for Noah, that by long meditation he might fix more deeply what he had learned by the word; partly for the wicked, that before dying they might feel the warnings they had derided were no empty threats — men who scorned God's patience a hundred years deserving to know they perished under a judgment they had treated as a fable. From this Calvin draws an observation about ourselves. God so tempers his judgments that men may have leisure to consider them; but the depravity of our nature shows in this, that when his anger is poured out suddenly we are stupefied, and when it advances at a measured pace we grow so accustomed to it as to despise it — because we do not willingly acknowledge God's hand without miracles. Wesley notes it rained without intermission or abatement, and on the whole earth at once; Clarke passes on Lightfoot's dating of the rain from the eighteenth of Marcheshvan to the twenty-eighth of Cisleu.

The repetition that follows Calvin defends as deliberate. Moses runs through the deluge briefly, yet returns to the same ground because the Spirit meant to hold our minds on a vengeance too terrible for language, and because nothing here is easy to believe — so it is inculcated the oftener, that however remote from our apprehension it may still obtain credit. The animals serve the same purpose: drawn from their woods and caverns by the faith of Noah as if led by the hand of God, each species preserved not by chance nor human industry, but because the Lord offered to Noah, from hand to hand, whatever he meant to keep alive. Henry hears in after his kind the language of the creation account, and takes it that just as many species were saved as created, and no more. But he adds a warning: when the occasion was over the restraint was lifted and the creatures were of the same kind as ever, for the ark did not alter their constitution — and hypocrites in the church, outwardly conforming to that ark's laws, may be as unchanged, as will appear one time or other.

The last clause is the one every commentator stops at. Henry gives the shutting two purposes: to secure Noah, the door shut close lest the waters break in and fast lest any break it down, so that God made him up as he makes up his jewels; and to exclude the rest, since hitherto the door had stood open and even in the last seven days a penitent might have been welcomed, whereas now God had shut it, and none can open. His comparison is the finest thing here: God put Adam into paradise but did not shut him in, and Adam threw himself out; putting Noah into the ark he shut him in — so when he brings a soul to Christ he secures its salvation, which is not in our keeping but in the Mediator's hand. Clarke says the same more grimly: as God shut him in he shut the others out, having waited a hundred and twenty years on a generation that did not repent. Ellicott finds the ascription remarkable, this act of personal care being assigned to Jehovah by name, whereas in the Chaldean Genesis the deity merely commands Xisuthrus to shut himself in. Calvin turns to the carpentry and finds it insufficient. That door must have been large which could admit an elephant, and no pitch would be tenacious enough to keep out the water through so many seams; Moses cuts off idle speculation by declaring the ark kept secure not by human artifice but by the secret power of God. Keil, surveying what follows, calls the description simple and majestic, the almighty judgment of God set beside the love manifest within it.
17:
Henry watches the water rise and reads the temper of those watching. The profane world, having refused to believe the flood would come, probably flattered themselves it would soon abate; but still it increased, still it prevailed. When God judges he will overcome: if he begin, he will make an end. And there is warning in the slowness — the gradual approaches of God's judgments, designed to bring sinners to repentance, are often abused instead to harden them. The depth he reckons at seven yards and a half, so that in vain was salvation hoped from hills: none of God's creatures stand so high that his power cannot overtop them. Then he turns to the vessel and gets two sentences worth the passage. The waters which broke down everything else bore up the ark — that which to unbelievers is a savour of death unto death being to the faithful a savour of life unto life; and the more the waters increased, the higher the ark rose toward heaven, so that sanctified afflictions are promotions. Wesley draws one dry inference: the mountains were covered, therefore mountains existed before the flood.

Ellicott takes the fifteen cubits for a measurement rather than a flourish — the draught of the ark, computed after it settled near Ararat. Twenty-two feet, then; and since the vessel floated on until it grounded, there must have been that depth even on the highest summit along its course. He doubts rain alone could account for it. Taking England's mean annual rainfall of thirty inches and supposing the whole of it to fall every twenty-four hours, forty days would yield some hundred feet — enough to strip the mountains of soil and dig new courses for the rivers. But water seeks the lower ground, and would have been doing so throughout, so it is hard to see how it could stand twenty-two feet deep on the heights without some cosmic convulsion carrying the waters from the equator toward the poles — which would also remove the difficulty of the ark being borne against the current up into Armenia. Clarke meets the objection by referring the doubter to Ray's Physico-theological Discourses.

Calvin explains why Moses dwells on the totality. The design is that we should not ascribe to fortune the flood by which the world perished, however customary it is for men to veil the works of God; since it is plainly declared that whatever flourished was destroyed, we infer a signal and indisputable judgment — especially as Noah alone remained secure, having embraced by faith the word in which salvation was contained. Two opposites are joined: the whole race destroyed, one family safe. From which we learn how profitable it was for Noah to disregard the world and obey God alone — recorded not to praise the man but to invite our imitation, and to teach us to bear the ridicule of the ungodly until the Lord shows by the issue that our obedience is approved. Peter makes that deliverance a figure of baptism, and the Church is justly compared to the ark; but the likeness holds, Calvin insists, only because drawn from the word of God — as Noah gathered his household on the strength of a promise, so we must renounce the world and die that the Lord may quicken us by his word; and the Papists act ridiculously who fabricate an ark without the word. Henry imagines the last hours outside it. Some climbed the tops of trees and spun out their terrors a while; some clung to the ark, hoping this might be their safety which they had so long made their sport; and some pleaded old acquaintance — have we not eaten and drunk in thy presence? — to which the answer could only be that he had called and they refused, and that God had shut the door, which Noah could not open.
22:
Two small qualifications close the account of the destruction. Clarke draws an inference from the phrase all that was in the dry land: only such animals as could not live in water were preserved in the ark, the rest needing no preservation. Gill enters the other caution, that every living substance destroyed cannot mean literally everything, since trees survived — after the waters abated there was an olive tree from which the dove brought a leaf — so the sentence must be read of the animals. Ellicott renders the phrase more exactly as everything that stood erect, and glosses the ground it was blotted from as the adamah, the portion subdued to his own use by the adam.

The hundred and fifty days then raise a chronological question the commentators answer in two ways. Gill reckons them not from the end of the forty days' rain but from the beginning of the flood, since from the seventeenth day of the second month, when the fountains were broken up, to the seventeenth of the seventh, when the ark rested on Ararat and the waters decreased, is exactly five months or a hundred and fifty days. That reckoning leaves him a difficulty, because the waters went on increasing after the rain had stopped; and he adopts Aben Ezra's solution, that there was continual rain afterwards, though less vehement, since otherwise the increase is not easy to account for. Clarke follows Lightfoot the other way and keeps the two sums distinct, the forty days not being included in the hundred and fifty, so that when the hundred and fifty were ended there were six months and ten days of the flood past. Ellicott takes Gill's side and states it most clearly: the rains lasted forty days, for a hundred and ten more the waters still bore up the ark, and then it grounded.

Ellicott alone reads the last verse for what it implies about the telling. The waters are said to have prevailed, which is literally that they were strong; and yet, though still mighty, they had by this time abated, since instead of covering the hills to a depth of nearly four fathoms they had let the ark touch dry land. That shift — the same word for strength used at a moment when the strength was demonstrably going out of them — suggests to him that the narrative is giving the personal experience of someone aboard, who would have known that the water was still deep and powerful but would also have felt the vessel take the ground. It is the same argument he makes about the exactness of the dates, which he thinks tradition could have carried correctly only for a short time before they had to be committed to writing, or confusion would inevitably have crept in.
